subject: english-literature
title: Landscape, Generations and the Second Half
welcome_lead: Trace the moorland landscape's symbolic work and analyse the often-overlooked second generation — young Cathy, Linton, Hareton.
meta_desc: A-Level OCR adventure on Wuthering Heights: moorland landscape, the second generation, and the novel's ambiguous resolution.
final_note: Brontë's second generation is not a moral correction but a haunted recurrence. The moors stay the same. The reader has to decide whether anything has actually been resolved.

concepts.def: The bleak Yorkshire upland between the Heights and the Grange; a Romantic-Gothic landscape that mirrors and resists human passion.
Wuthering Heights (high, windswept, primitive) and Thrushcross Grange (low, enclosed, civilised); Brontë's spatial dialectic.
Young Cathy Linton, Linton Heathcliff, Hareton Earnshaw; their narrative occupies the second half of the novel.
Educated by Cathy after Heathcliff's death; his learning to read symbolises the second generation's tentative repair.
Catherine's marginalia, Hareton's illiteracy, Linton's letters — books and writing structure power across the novel.
The final image — sleepers in 'that quiet earth' — is undercut by the shepherd boy's report of ghosts walking; resolution is denied.

walkthroughs.body_html: The novel's geography is dialectical: Wuthering Heights sits high on the moors, its name (Lockwood explains in Ch. 1) referring to the 'tumult' of its weather. Thrushcross Grange sits four miles below in a sheltered park. The two houses figure opposed modes of life: passionate/primitive vs civilised/enclosed. Critics including Q.D. Leavis read the novel as a spatial morality play; the second generation's traffic between houses reorders the moral map.

The second half tracks Catherine and Heathcliff's daughter (young Cathy, born 1784) and Hindley's son (Hareton). Heathcliff degrades Hareton in revenge for Hindley's earlier treatment of him; he forces Cathy into marriage with his weakling son Linton. After Heathcliff's death (1802), Cathy teaches Hareton to read. Critics including Carol Jacobs and Lyn Pykett debate whether this is reparative or merely cyclical. The novel resists either consolation.

Lockwood's final paragraph contemplates the three graves — Catherine, Edgar, Heathcliff — and wonders 'how any one could ever imagine unquiet slumbers for the sleepers in that quiet earth'. But Nelly has just reported the shepherd boy who saw Heathcliff and 'a woman' on the moor. The two endings cancel each other. Critics including J. Hillis Miller make this the novel's defining figure: meaning withheld. AO5 reward goes to candidates who can name and inhabit this ambiguity.
